chapter_theme: Natrinai 361 to 380: returns read in mullai garlands, bells and herdsmen's flutes, with the wife eager to feast guests; the hill girl's millet field closing as mothers sense the secret and the friend warns or threatens publicity; a lover's madal and an eloper who will fight strangers but hide from her kin; shore laments at evening; and in marutham a husband's tender memory of his wife's lying-in set against the friend's use of the same motherhood to refuse his bard.

361.reading: The friend, answering the go-betweens, says the tall man's chariot has come home at evening to the fragrant house: he and his young men wear the small-flowered mullai, his gold-harnessed horses run as if crossing the sky, his long-tongued bells ring through the rain-cooled scrub, and the woman of fine jewels, her long ache put away, is now eager to feast guests.
361.nuance: The proof of the return is a garland, not a sight of the man: the friend tells the go-betweens that even his young men wear the mullai, so the waiting is over and their errand is not needed; the wife's wish to feast guests is the sign that the house is whole again.

colophon.thurai: வாயில்களோடு தோழி உறழ்ந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-cooled scrub at evening and the mullai garland of the returning man

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressees are the go-betweens (வாயில்கள்) whom she disputes with

362.reading: The eloping man tells the girl who moved like a crafted doll and crossed the bounds of her father's house that she may play a while, watching and gathering the red velvet mites spread over the forest that the first cool rains have adorned, while he leans on the broad trunk of a vengai rubbed by a young elephant: if a fight comes he will not fear but drive it off, and if her own people come he will hide.
362.nuance: His courage has a precise limit: strangers he will fight, her kin he will hide from, because a blow against her people would end the marriage the flight is meant to make; the road is offered to her as a playground of red mites, not a waste.

colophon.thurai: உடன்போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the flight from her father's house decides it, though the forest is green with first rain

363.reading: The friend tells the lord of the full-watered shore that if he takes leave saying he will go to his clear-sea country of backwater fields hedged with kandal, he should come back bringing the sand of the ford with which the tireless smith fuses broken links, for yesterday at fine evening, with him, her green leaf-skirt was torn, her garland faded, a few bright bangles slipped, and the anklet of the girl who made the crabs dance was crushed.
363.nuance: The torn skirt, faded garland, loosened bangles and crushed anklet are the evidence of the day's meeting that the house will read; the friend's demand for the smith's fusing sand is a half-joking order to undo the damage before anyone sees it.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி தலைமகளை என்னை ஆற்றுவிக்குமென்று ஆகாதோ எம்பெருமான் கவலாது செல்வது யான் ஆற்றுவிக்குமிடத்துக் கவன்றால் நீ ஆற்றுவி எனச் சொல்லியது கையுறை நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் கையுறை உரைத்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: kandal hedge, backwater and crabs of the shore

364.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the season he named is past, and at midnight the roaring sky moves heavy with water in the mist and the cold north wind brings misery; if a few more such days pass she will not live many more, when in turn the sweet bells with small red tongues that never knew thunder ring near the town, and the unlettered herdsmen who brought home the many cows play sweet kondrai flutes in every common, in the evening that hurries life away, if it comes together with the faultless rain.
364.nuance: The thunder and the midnight storm she can bear; it is the softest sounds, bells too small to know thunder and the flutes of unlearned herdsmen, that she says will take her life, because they mark the evening hour of homecoming in which he does not come.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் பிரிவிடை மெலிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the named season, the rain and the herdsmen's evening

365.reading: The friend, with the hero standing unseen nearby, tells the heroine: let us slip mother's strict watch, pass the great door, go into the common and, in daylight before everyone, ask aloud the way to his town of wide fields, and tell the lord of the sky-touching hill, whose slopes roar with falls even when the clouds have not rained for many days, 'you are not a man of worth', and come back.
365.nuance: The hill gives water when the sky gives none, and the reproach lies in the gap: its lord does not give even what is due. The threat is to make the secret public in daylight, the one step a woman of the house is not supposed to take; a near miss for ullurai, since only one pair (the hill's unfailing falls, his failing presence) can be named.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தலைமகட்கு உரைப்பாளாய் இயற்பழித்துஇன்னது செய்தும் என்பாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord of waterfalls

366.reading: The man tells his heart, set on leaving for wealth, that those who part from the girl with great shoulders, whose fine cloth lets her many-stranded girdle gleam through like a rising snake, whose gem-dark hair is washed clean and tied with short-stemmed cold-season mullai visited by bees, and leave her soft bed in the north wind that opens the spear-white buds of the sugarcane and shakes the nest the wise sparrow toiled to hang from the bamboo, are fools, and long live this world.
366.nuance: The argument is made by season rather than by road: the cold wind that would lash the traveller is the same wind that rocks a sparrow's hard-built nest, so the poem ends on the general maxim the colophon calls உலகியல், that leavers are fools.

colophon.thurai: உலகியல் கூறிப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிய வலித்த நெஞ்சிற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: leaving for wealth is weighed and refused

iraicchi.act: the wise little sparrow labours to build its nest and keeps to it while the north wind shakes it on the bamboo
iraicchi.sense: even a small bird holds to the home it built when the cold wind blows, so a man who leaves his wife's bed in that wind is a fool

367.reading: The friend tells the soft girl: in the far-famed little village of Aruman's old house, where the sharp-beaked hen of the crooked-eyed crow, gathering her trembling-winged chick and calling her kin, snatches the white rice of red paddy with dark fried meat along with the offering to the fierce god and sits in flocks at the house rich in food, the young men have come wearing a cool garland of open mullai bound with blue lily, like the one in your thick dark hair, and our man too, driving fine horses with spread manes, will come without fail this dewy day.
367.nuance: The crow hen gathering her chick and kin to the house's food is read traditionally as the omen of a coming guest; here it does not pass the act test cleanly (her feeding is not something the wife does or fails to do) and is left as scene, a near miss for iraicchi. The proof is again the retinue's garland.

colophon.thurai: வரவு மலிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the returning retinue's mullai garland

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the voice that calls her அரிவை and says நமரும் is the friend's

368.reading: The friend tells the hero: what is sweeter than driving small parrots from the great field, swinging on the black-stemmed vengai and playing with you in leaf-skirts and coming home? But mother, seeing the wild fragrance in her coiled dark hair and the pallor spreading on her small forehead, her heart sinking for no clear reason, hinting at something else, sighed hot breaths; sir, we are afraid, we are to be pitied.
368.nuance: The mother never accuses; she reads two signs, the strange scent in the hair and the pallor, says something else, and sighs, and that silence is what tells the friend the girl will be kept indoors. The joy of the first four lines exists to be lost.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகற்குச் செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: millet field, parrots and vengai swing

369.reading: The heroine tells her friend that as the sun's anger cools and it reaches the hill, flocks of herons with full wings rise and stream across the sky, the day slowly passes and the mullai buds open their mouths in the great dim evening; if this comes again today she does not know, does not know, how she will swim across her love, which breaks her restraint as the fierce flood of the Ganga, falling from the shining white falls of the sky on the Himalaya's peak where ñemai trees rise, overruns its banks and breaks the dams.
369.nuance: The simile is built as a pun: the flood breaks dams (சிறை அடு) and her love breaks restraint (நிறை அடு), so the far-off Ganga falling from the Himalaya measures a feeling at the evening shore. She does not ask how to stop the flood but how to swim it.

colophon.thurai: பட்ட பின்றை வரையாது பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகள் வன்புறை எதிர் அழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: her lament at evening with the shore's herons; the mullai buds are of another land

370.reading: The man, whose wife's sulking has gone on too long, says: come, bard, let us laugh; when she who had helped our clan with her heavy pregnancy among her kin lay in the bright house shining with mustard seed glistening with ghee, and, having borne a son, changed her name and became, with her lined waist, an 'old woman', I came near saying 'are you asleep, soft one of thin locks?', laid a blue lily on her lovely belly and stood thinking, and she saw me, slowly showed a smile shy as a bud, and covered her flower-like painted eyes with her hand.
370.nuance: The joke he invites the bard to share is his wife's new title, 'old woman', given her by the birth of a son, and her shyness at being found by him in the lying-in room; in a marutham poem of oodal the tenderest scene is told as his evidence that she is still the bashful girl he married.

colophon.thurai: ஊடல் நீட ஆற்றானாய் நின்றான் பாணர்க்குச் சொல்லியது முன் நிகழ்ந்ததனைப் பாணர்க்குச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's memory used against a long sulk

371.reading: The man returning with his work done tells his charioteer: like kondrai on a hill of kaayaa, lightning flashes so that the clefts of the great mountain shine, and the cloud that had not rained, looking toward the land where his dark girl lives, has spread to cover the wide sky and begun to rain; she, her bright bangles slipping, sighs and has begun to burn; and against that the herdsmen have begun their flutes, in the night of roaring thunder.
371.nuance: Three verbs of beginning (தொடங்கினவே, தொடங்கினளே, தொடங்கினரே) run in parallel: the rain begins, she begins to burn, the herdsmen begin to play; he imagines her evening at the very hour it starts, which is why the chariot must hurry.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்றான் பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the rains begun over the kaayaa hills and the herdsmen's flutes

comparisons.tenor: lightning on the dark cloud over the hill

372.reading: The heroine, knowing she is to be kept indoors and speaking for the hero to overhear, tells her friend it is ruinous: on the backwater the honey-full overripe fruit of the grove's palm falls, crushing the broad-petalled neythal, its tip breaking, and sinks deep in the dark mire so the flock of herons flees, at the shore of the lord who, on the white sand like the curve of a conch, looked at her sweetly with a willing heart; and they say, fearing she would grieve as when the swaying white thing mother gave was broken, her people tell her not to grieve over what has come, in the good town hedged with kandal where cold-headed fishermen at home count the lights of the sturdy boats that search the dark backwater.
372.nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the ripe palm fruit that crushes the neythal and scares off the herons invites the reading of a love that has fallen on her and set the town talking, but only one pair can be named with confidence and the poem does not anchor it. Lines 8 to 10 are obscure.

colophon.thurai: மேல் இற்செறிப்பான் அறிந்து ஆற்றாளாகி நின்ற தலைமகள் ஆற்ற வேண்டி உலகியல் மேல் வைத்துச் சிறைப்புறமாகச் செறியார் எனச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, neythal flower and fishermen

373.reading: The friend asks whether it will be ours tomorrow too, the joy of the girl of the hills who sang of her father's dark cloud-capped mountain as she pounded white hill-paddy while the grey-headed monkey scattered the fallen jackfruit segments in the yard, bathing with the man of the land in the falls of the god-haunted slope, and climbing the built platform on the vengai whose rain-opened buds tell the season, to drive the green flock from the curved ears of the small millet.
373.nuance: The whole poem is one long relative clause hanging on the final question, so the day's meeting is listed in full as something that may not happen again; the warning of confinement is never stated, only implied by நாளையும் 'tomorrow too'.

colophon.thurai: செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: hill girl, vengai platform and millet field

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; நமக்கே takes the heroine in, and the warning is meant for the hero

374.reading: The man returning with his work done asks the wayfarers with tall umbrellas, who quell their hunger with the fruit of the salt-land tamarind on the unfinished road of hard gravel, by the little village crowded with salt merchants, whether he still has what he had before, and then how it is with the sweet-spoken girl of fine jewels who, eager to feast guests, suffers as the water from her long hair dressed with dark gems wets her freckled breast.
374.nuance: Line 5 is compressed: he seems to ask whether the life he had before still waits for him, and only then to ask after her; the formula 'eager to feast guests' (also natrinai 361) shows she keeps the house ready while she weeps.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீள்வான் இடைச் சுரத்துக் கண்டார்க்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waiting at home for his return; the road itself is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressees are travellers met on the waste (இடைச் சுரத்துக் கண்டார்)

375.reading: The friend tells the lord of the full-watered shore of many-flowered groves, where the long-branched punnai drops fragrant pollen and the flocks of crested herons move off, that since he lacks love it would be good if he came in a way that gladdened the girl of fine brow, who desired him with her senses, and me and her shame together, to our town of high sand gardens, where at the head of night, when the moon has moved, the strong waves come as if they were hurling themselves.
375.nuance: 'Come so that her shame too rejoices' means come openly, as a suitor: a coming that pleases shame is a wedding, not a tryst. The reading of lines 4 and 5 is uncertain in its syntax.

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்தொழுக தலைமகளது நிலை உணர்ந்த தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, herons and the shore grove

376.reading: The friend, with the hero standing unseen, tells the curve-beaked green parrots who eat together with their kin, as freely as the hill lord gives, the red millet with green stalks whose heads droop like the bent trunk of a winnow-eared elephant: if you see the man with the good garland on his chest, a cool wet chaplet of kullai, kulavi, koothalam and blue lily woven with illam, a bow bound round, appearing by the asoka, tell him plainly so he knows that our mother without justice, afflicting like an affliction, will not stop guarding the empty field.
376.nuance: The parrots share their millet as the hill lord shares his wealth, which flatters the overhearing hero and hints at what he should do; the harvested field still guarded by the mother means the meeting place is closed.

colophon.thurai: தோழி கிளிமேல் வைத்துச் சிறைப்புறமாகச் செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: millet, parrots and the asoka of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the parrots eating with their kin

377.reading: The man, turned away, says within the friend's hearing: shall we, riding the palm-stem horse and wearing a garland, praising the beauty of the bright-browed girl through lands and towns of wide spaces, intent on doing it and suffering hard, not die of it as of a sickness? Her lovely forehead fringed with curls, like the wide light of the green-rayed moon that the snake has bitten into in the vast dark sky, chides and wastes me and has become my disease.
377.nuance: Riding the madal would put him in perunthinai; here it is still a threat spoken for the friend's ears, so the poem stays in kalavu. The eclipse simile is exact: the dark curls bite into the bright forehead as the snake bites the moon.

colophon.thurai: சேட்படுக்கப்பட்டு ஆற்றானாகிய தலைமகன் தோழி கேட்ப தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the madal threat of a hill lover turned away; the poem gives no land of its own

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks within himself (தன்னுள்ளே) for the friend to hear

378.reading: The friend, with the hero standing unseen, tells the heroine: the night watch is long, the backwater is long, and love grows and lets the eyes not close, as the clear sea's roaring waves, slow as a drum's beat, toss like men with an old wound; though these afflict us, nowhere does day come after the night, and the neighbours' wives sing of her pallor with gossiping mouths; this, friend, is the measure of the bond formed without inquiry with the lord of the cold shore loud with sound, trusting the humble words he spoke, touching us to comfort us, after he came and ruined our little striped sand-house.
378.nuance: Three long things open the poem, the watch, the backwater and love, and the ending names its cause in a word of the ethics books: a friendship made without inquiry (நாடாது). The ruined sand-house is the girls' play, so the courtship began as a boy's prank on their game.

colophon.thurai: தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது தலைமகன் ஒருவழித் தணந்த பின்னை வன்புறை எதிர்மொழிந்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, sea and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the second alternative makes it the heroine's reply to her friend's reassurance

379.reading: The friend tells the hero that when the strong untaught young of the grey-headed monkey, not leaving the yard by the hill, clung to the low branch of the vengai with flower clusters like leaping flame and snatched the honey-sweet milk from her hand, the hill girl wept till the painted beauty of her eyes was spoiled, and they became like the blue lilies that bloom wet in the rain-filled moat at the gate of Kudanthai of the Cholas rich in chariots, and her fingers, beating her lovely belly without stopping, reddened like the plump buds of kanthal flowering on the dark slopes of high-peaked Pothiyil where clouds drift.
379.nuance: A child's grief over stolen milk is drawn with two royal similes, a Chola moat and the Pothiyil hill, so the friend's report of the girl's simplicity is also a portrait of her beauty; told to the hero, it says she is too young to be left waiting.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகளை மடமை கூறியது காப்புக் கைம்மிக்க காலத்துத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, vengai and the hill girl

380.reading: The friend refuses the bard: our clothes and shoulders are soiled with ghee and the smoke of seasoning, sweet milk oozes from our soft spotted breasts, and holding our son we smell of new birth; we are no match for the chariot-man who shows himself in the street of brightly jewelled women; so, bard, though you can raise your small lute of sweet voice with strings like gold, do not bow, take your lord of the cool ford and go; even the horses that stand long tire of the harness while he is kept from the singing houses; do not speak artless words where we have no wish.
380.nuance: The refusal is made with the body of new motherhood itself: the ghee, the smoke, the milk and the smell of birth are offered as the reason she cannot compete with the jewelled women, which is both humility and accusation. Lines 10 and 11 are compressed.

colophon.thurai: பாணற்குத் தோழி வாயில் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: refusal of the go-between bard for a husband who visits courtesans

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the first-person plural speaks for the house

links.note: Both poems close on the same formula for the waiting wife, விருந்து அயர் விருப்பினள் with திருந்துஇழை: in 361 the friend reports it as the wife's state once the chariot is home; in 374 the returning husband imagines it on the road, joined to வருந்தும், her suffering.
links.teaches: The same line serves as the end of waiting in one poem and as the husband's picture of waiting in the other, so the wish to feast guests was a fixed sign of the wife who keeps the house ready, and whether it is joy or grief depends only on whether the chariot has arrived.

links.note: The eloping man in Natrinai 362 vows that if a fight comes he will not fear and will drive it off, but if her kin come he will hide (நுமர் வரின் மறைகுவென்); Pattinathar's antadhi verse 922 gives the hero the same two conditions, hill men he will make food for kites, but if they are her kin he will hide (உமராயின் மறைகுவனே).
links.teaches: Pattinathar kept not only the eloping lover's boast but its exact limit, courage against strangers and concealment before her family, which shows the devotional kovai inherited the Sangam udanpokku speech as a fixed thurai with its own logic, since striking her kin would undo the marriage the flight is meant to make.

links.note: Kural 1228 has the waiting woman say the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Natrinai 364's heroine says the herdsmen's kondrai flutes and the cattle bells at evening will take her life if they come with the rain after the named season has passed.
links.teaches: The couplet's flute that kills is given its setting by the Natrinai poem, cows driven home, bells that never knew thunder and the season he named already gone, which shows why a sweet pastoral sound became deadly: it marks the homecoming hour, and the season promise turns it into proof that he has not come.

links.note: In 371 the returning hero tells his charioteer that the rain has begun toward where she lives, that she has begun to burn and the herdsmen have begun their flutes; in 364 the heroine herself says the herdsmen's flutes in the rainy evening will take her life.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems show the man's guess on the road matching what the woman says at home almost sound for sound, so the herdsmen's evening flute was a shared code in mullai by which each partner knew the other's hour, and the hero's haste is grounded in knowing exactly how that evening falls on her.

links.note: Kural 1137 holds that nothing is nobler than a woman who suffers a sea of desire yet does not ride the madal, that is, does not make her love public; in Natrinai 365 the friend proposes that they slip the mother's watch, go to the common in daylight before everyone and ask the way to his town to rebuke him.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the woman's silence a virtue, but the Natrinai friend uses the threat of breaking it, a daylight public walk being the woman's form of the madal, as a lever on the overhearing hero, so the restraint the Kural praises was also a weapon that worked only while it might be dropped.

links.note: In Akananuru 167 the man tells his heart, which is pressing him to leave for wealth, that after a sweet night with his wife in the tall house he would lie sleepless in a ruined village hall, and gives up the journey; in Natrinai 366 he tells his heart that whoever leaves her washed, flower-tied hair and soft bed in the north wind that shakes the sparrow's nest is a fool.
links.teaches: The two give the same refusal two arguments: Akananuru 167 sets the home against the terror of the road, while Natrinai 366 never reaches the road and argues from the season alone, a cold wind that even a bird's home must withstand, so the stay-at-home decision could rest either on fear or on a general law of the world (உலகியல்).

links.note: In 367 the friend tells the heroine that the young men have come wearing a garland of mullai and blue lily and that her man will surely come today; in 361 the friend reports that he himself and his young men are wearing mullai as his chariot reaches the house.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the two poems show that the mullai garland was the badge of the returning party, worn first by the retinue as a herald and then by the master on arrival, so the friend could promise the return from the young men's flowers before any chariot was seen.

links.note: Kural 1251 has the woman say love's axe breaks the door of restraint (நிறை) barred with shame; Natrinai 369's heroine, left unmarried while he seeks wealth, says she cannot swim across a love that breaks her restraint (நிறை அடு காமம்) like the Ganga in flood breaking dams.
links.teaches: Both name the same loss, restraint broken by love, but the Kural's image is a single blow to a closed door while the Natrinai's is a flood from the Himalaya that keeps coming each evening, so the poem adds what the couplet lacks: that the breaking recurs at a fixed hour and the woman's question is endurance, how to swim, not resistance.

links.note: In 370 the husband recalls his wife in the lying-in room, smeared with ghee and mustard, newly called 'old woman' after bearing a son, and finds her shy smile the sweetest thing; in 380 the friend says the wife's ghee-soiled clothes, milk-wet breasts and smell of new birth make her no match for the jewelled women he visits.
links.teaches: The same marks of motherhood are the husband's proof of tenderness in one poem and the wife's side's proof of his desertion in the other, which shows that the marutham quarrel is fought over what a mother's body means, and that the husband's memory in 370 is an answer to exactly the charge 380 makes.

links.note: Kural 1268 has the man, held by the king's war, wish that the king win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast for guests; Natrinai 374's man, returning from his work, asks travellers about the wife who longs to feast guests yet weeps.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the feast for guests as the man's own goal after duty, while the Natrinai poem puts the same wish in the wife and shows it unfulfilled in her tears, so the household's guest-feast was the shared picture of reunion that each partner ascribed to the other.

links.note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily and carrying a bow, coming to the swing by the asoka and the harvested millet field and finding them deserted; in Natrinai 376 she tells the parrots to tell the man with the garland and bow who appears by the asoka that the mother still guards even the empty field.
links.teaches: Together they show the harvested millet field as the clock of the kalavu plot: once the crop is cut the daytime meeting place is gone, and the friend's two messages, where our village is in Akananuru 38 and the guard that stays on the empty field in Natrinai 376, both push the man to come openly as a suitor.

links.note: In Kural 1133 the turned-away man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal that lovers ride; in Natrinai 377 the turned-away man, speaking for the friend to hear, asks whether riding the madal and praising the girl through lands and towns will not kill him like a disease.
links.teaches: The Kural states what the madal costs the man, his shame, while the Natrinai shows what it would do, carry her beauty's praise through every town, so the threat works on the friend because his loss of shame would become the girl's public exposure.

links.note: Kural 791 says nothing is as ruinous as making a friend without inquiry, since the devoted cannot leave once the bond is made; Natrinai 378 ends with the friend (or the heroine) calling her sleepless nights and the neighbours' gossip the measure of the bond made without inquiry (நாடாது இயைந்த நண்பு) with the lord of the shore.
links.teaches: The akam poem applies the ethics book's rule for choosing friends to a love made at a girl's sand-house, and its suffering shows the second half of the couplet at work, that she cannot leave the bond once made, so the maxim on friendship was available as a verdict on unwise love.

source_issues: 364 lines 4 and 12, 367 lines 4 and 8, 380 line 1: line repaired for the lost vowel sign of -ஒடு, as show flags.

363: the first colophon alternative describes a speech in which the friend reassures the departing hero that she will console the heroine, which the verse does not contain; the verse asks him to bring the smith's sand for a crushed anklet. Copied as it stands; the verse is marked uncertain.
367: the colophon (வரவு மலிந்தது) names no speaker; the friend is inferred from the verse.
siddhar:922: the shared index reading says the hero 'will not hide', but the Tamil ends உமராயின் மறைகுவனே, 'if they are your kin I will hide'; the link from natrinai 362 follows the Tamil.
